sources.name: Office for National Statistics
sources.text: Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew, "Changes to National Accounts: Inclusion of Illegal Drugs and Prostitution in the UK National Accounts", 29 May 2014. The link is a mirror on the UN Statistical Institute for Asia and the Pacific training site; the ONS original URL no longer resolves. The PDF carries the ONS header, authors and date. Supports: GNI's use in EU budget contributions and the 2012 audit's areas for improvement due by 2014; ESA95 section 1.13 and the footnote "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10"; the executive summary on "significant limitations in the availability of data" and assumptions on which the estimates are "partly based", "especially" for prostitution; Eaves' approx 7,000 off-street estimate for London in 2004 and how it was made; the Metropolitan Police's 115 on the street "at any one time"; scaling to "c. 58,000"; "there is no time series" and variation by the male population and the CPI for personal services; clients per week of 20, 25 and 30 following "a Netherlands assumption"; £55 in 2004 from Punternet, footnote 12 pointing to a Wikipedia page; the assumptions labelled "weak" and "controversial"; the drugs assumptions quoted in the body; "probably false" (4 occurrences).

sources.name: Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser
sources.text: "Sex, Drugs and GDP", Civil Service Quarterly blog, 15 October 2014: "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!)"; illegal activities contributing "up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP"; "legally mandated through the European System of Accounts 2010"; "Comparability between nations dictates that all countries include it in their GDP figures."

sources.name: Office for National Statistics
sources.text: Freedom of information response, "Illegal Production (N2)", released 6 November 2015: total N2 for 2010 of £9,097 million; N2 as 0.58% of GDP, drugs 0.24%, prostitution 0.35%; prostitution in COICOP 12.2, "The value for 2010 is £5.6bn (current prices), which is 0.4% of GDP."

sources.name: Office for National Statistics
sources.text: "Revisions to gross domestic product in Blue Book 2016": the reduction of prostitution estimates "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes"; "Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

sources.name: Office for National Statistics
sources.text: Time series MNC8, "12.2 Prostitution CP NSA £m", dataset BB, released 31 October 2025: household final consumption expenditure on prostitution, current prices, 1985 to 2024. Supports the chart, the 2010 value of £4,370m, and 2019 £5,993m, 2020 £4,130m, 2024 £6,431m.
